accuracy.evidence: Definitions and results checked against the Pearson Edexcel and OCR A level Mathematics specifications (discrete random variables) and CCSS S-MD.2, plus Rice's Mathematical Statistics and Data Analysis ch. 4 (expectation, linearity E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b, law of large numbers). Every number recomputed: prize game 10 × 0.1 = 1; dice 21/6 = 3.5; points card 0.5 + 0.6 + 1.0 = 2.1; raffle −2 × 0.7 + 3 × 0.2 + 18 × 0.1 = −1.4 + 0.6 + 1.8 = 1.0 (gains net of the £2 ticket); fair stakes 5 × 0.1 = 0.50, 6 × 1/6 = 1, 3 × 1/3 = 1; dice E(X + 10) = 13.5, E(2X) = 7, E(2X + 1) = 8; challenge −£0.50, 2.3, 5, 10, −£30. The seeded 1000-roll simulation ends at a mean of 3.52 with visible early wobble (3.3 at 10 rolls, 3.03 at 100). Parameterised answers w/10, w/5 − s, a/4 and 2e + b are exact to 2 dp at every corner.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented errors in expectation (Garfield & Ben-Zvi, Developing Students' Statistical Reasoning; Konold's outcome approach; examiner reports on A level S1/statistics papers): unweighted averaging of values (the 'Average the x values' trap in the table step, tag eqw, p3 and m7), taking the middle or the mode as E(X) (beam feedback for pivot at the midpoint or mode, tags mid and mode), expecting E(X) to be a possible or most likely outcome (long-run prediction options, tags likely and outcome, p4), forgetting the stake or subtracting it only on a win (fair-price step, tags stake and prob, m6), and misapplying linearity as 2E(X) or E(X) + 1 (scale-and-shift wrong answers 7 and 4.5, tags shift and scale, p5).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagexpv is built around expectation: a probability beam whose pivot must be dragged to the balance point for three distributions and that tilts by Σ p(x − pivot), an x·P(X = x) table for a £2 raffle with an unweighted-average trap, a seeded running-mean plot of 1000 dice rolls on a log axis against the E(X) line, a stake slider showing E(gain) = w·p − stake for three games, and a scale-and-shift picker for E(aX + b). It differs from flagpdist (building distributions), flagexpf (expected frequency np) and flagsumone (probabilities summing to 1); the gate reports under 30% shingle overlap with every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea is found by doing before it is named: the beam only levels at Σ x·P, so learners discover that rare large values pull the mean; the table makes them multiply and add (and shows why plain averaging gives 6.33); the run shows the mean settling to 3.5 though 3.5 is never rolled; the stake slider shows the expected gain falling to 0 exactly when stake = expected prize; and the three linearity questions build E(aX + b) = a·E(X) + b. Step summaries appear only after the task.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each with a tempting wrong option that the lab disproves: £5 (the middle value) for the 1-in-10 £10 game, which the beam rejects at 5 and balances at 1; 'Yes, sometimes' or 'the most likely score' for rolling 3.5, which the simulation never produces while its mean converges; and +£4.00 (prize minus stake) or £0 for the £1 game, which the stake slider shows is −£0.50. The task message echoes the locked-in choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with two wrong options each and a distinct message per slip: mid, mode, eqw, likely, outcome, stake, prob, shift, scale, total and zero (e.g. '£10 − £2 = £8 is what you gain only when you win. You win just 15% of the time.'). In-lab wrong moves also name the slip: pivot at the middle value, pivot at the mode, adding before all rows are in, the unweighted average, a free game, an overpriced stake, and each wrong linearity answer.

readability.evidence: validate_lessons.py passes the learner limits (kid FK under 6.5, adult under 9.5). The kid text works through one £10 game in plain words before naming E(X) as a long-run mean; the adult text uses the exact A level terms: discrete random variable, expectation, E(X) = Σ x·P(X = x), expected gain, fair game, linearity, law of large numbers.

no_filler.evidence: No filler pattern matches. Each lab step carries one idea (balance point, Σ x·P, long run, fair price, linearity) and every feedback line contains a calculation or a rule. Item explanations show the working and name the trap answer where it helps (e.g. '8 forgets the + 3, and 7 forgets to double').

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px in light and dark, before and after Show me on every step. The beam, table rows (about 40 px tall), running-mean plot and stake slider fit at 360 px with labels readable; probability labels sit above each bar and the pivot label below the axis. The buttons below the canvas ('◀ 1', '◀ 0.1', '0.1 ▶', '1 ▶', 'Balance here', row buttons, 'Roll 10/100', 'Stake ±10p') wrap onto two rows without clipping.

accessibility.evidence: Everything can be done with buttons as well as drag/tap: pivot nudges and 'Balance here', one button per table row plus 'Add the products', roll buttons, 'Stake −10p'/'Stake +10p'/'Lock in stake', and one button per linearity answer. The canvas aria-label describes the state after each move ('Prize game. Values 0, 10. Pivot at 0. The beam tips right.', 'Win £5 with probability 0.1. Stake £0.90. Expected gain −£0.40.'). Challenge feedback is an aria-live status. walk.cjs reports axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) clean in light and dark on desktop and iPhone 13 with no console errors.
